description:
Phallus impudicus, the Common Stinkhorn, is a widespread saprotrophic fungus famous for its rapid, phallic fruiting body and the powerful, fetid odor it emits at maturity. The fungus first appears as a partly buried whitish to off-white "egg" 4-6 cm across, attached to the soil by a white mycelial cord (rhizomorph). From this egg the fruiting body erupts rapidly, the spongy white stalk (receptacle) elongating to 10-25 cm in a matter of hours. The stalk is capped with a thimble-like, ridged/honeycombed cap coated in a slimy, olive-green to brown spore mass called the gleba. The gleba smells strongly of carrion/rotting flesh, attracting flies and other insects that feed on it and disperse the spores; once the slime is removed by insects the underlying white cap is exposed. It is a common species of woodlands, gardens, hedgerows, mulched beds, and wood-debris-rich soils across Europe, North America, and beyond, fruiting mainly in summer and autumn.

EDIBILITY AND SAFETY: Only the immature "egg" stage is eaten, and only as a regional novelty. When sliced, the egg reveals a firm white outer skin, a thick gelatinous (jelly-like) layer, and a darker olive-green embryonic gleba/stalk in the center. The crisp inner core is sometimes eaten raw (reportedly radish-like) or cooked; the gelatinous layer is typically peeled away. The mature stinkhorn, with its slimy gleba, is not eaten. CRITICAL CUT TEST: an unopened stinkhorn egg can superficially resemble the egg/button (volva-enclosed young fruiting body) of a deadly Amanita such as the Death Cap (Amanita phalloides) or Destroying Angel (Amanita virosa). ALWAYS slice any white "egg" vertically from top to bottom before considering it: a stinkhorn egg shows a gelatinous layer surrounding an undifferentiated olive embryonic structure, whereas an Amanita button shows a clearly differentiated, developing gilled mushroom (cap, gills, stem) in cross-section. If a young gilled mushroom is visible inside, discard it — it is not a stinkhorn. When in doubt, do not eat.
edibilityNotes: Edible only at the immature white "egg" stage, and only as a regional novelty; the crisp inner core is eaten raw (radish-like flavor) or cooked, with the gelatinous outer layer peeled away. The mature stalk with its foul-smelling olive gleba is not consumed. SAFETY-CRITICAL: an unopened white stinkhorn egg can resemble the button of a deadly Amanita (Death Cap, Destroying Angel). Always slice the egg vertically before eating — a stinkhorn shows a gelatinous layer around an olive embryonic gleba with no gills, while an Amanita button reveals a developing gilled mushroom inside. If any gill structure is present, discard it. If uncertain, do not eat.
distribution: Widespread across Europe and North America, and reported from other temperate regions of the world.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita phalloides (Death Cap)
dangerousLookalikes.note: The deadly Death Cap emerges from a white volval egg/button that can resemble a stinkhorn egg. Slice vertically: an Amanita button reveals a developing gilled mushroom (cap, gills, stem), whereas a stinkhorn egg shows a gelatinous layer around an undifferentiated olive embryonic gleba with no gills.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Amanita virosa (Destroying Angel)
dangerousLookalikes.note: Another deadly white Amanita whose young volva-enclosed button can be mistaken for a stinkhorn egg. The vertical cut test distinguishes them: gilled mushroom inside = Amanita (discard); gelatinous olive embryo with no gills = stinkhorn.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Mutinus caninus (Dog Stinkhorn)
dangerousLookalikes.note: A related, smaller and more slender stinkhorn that also arises from an egg; harmless but distinguished by its narrower orange-tipped stalk and weaker odor.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Phallus hadriani (Dune Stinkhorn)
dangerousLookalikes.note: A very similar stinkhorn arising from a pinkish/purple-tinged egg, typically in dunes and sandy soils; also edible at the egg stage and not dangerous, but worth distinguishing for accurate ID.
